# Chapter 11 Practice: Intermolecular Forces, Liquids, and Solids

*Auto-generated from the assessment guide (`assessment-support/intermolecular-forces.md`), grouped by objective. 27 questions spanning multiple-choice, short-answer, and workout formats.*

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 1
{{sp[info] Objective 11.1a}} · *multiple-choice* Which intermolecular forces are present in $\ce{CH3F}$ (fluoromethane)?

(A) Dispersion only
(B) Dipole-dipole and dispersion only
\(C) Hydrogen bonding, dipole-dipole, and dispersion
(D) Hydrogen bonding only
:::
::: tab Answer
**(B)** Fluoromethane is polar (C–F bond), so dipole-dipole and dispersion forces apply. However, its hydrogen atoms are bonded to *carbon*, not to F, N, or O — hydrogen bonding requires H bonded directly to one of those three atoms, which is not the case here.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 2
{{sp[info] Objective 11.1a}} · *short answer* Explain why $\ce{NH3}$ can hydrogen-bond with itself, but $\ce{PH3}$ (same group, one row down) cannot.
:::
::: tab Answer
Hydrogen bonding requires H bonded directly to N, O, or F — small, highly electronegative atoms. Nitrogen qualifies; phosphorus, despite being in the same group, is larger and less electronegative, so P–H bonds are not polar enough (and P is not small enough) to produce a hydrogen bond. $\ce{PH3}$ has only dipole-dipole and dispersion forces, which is why it boils at −87.7 °C versus $\ce{NH3}$'s −33.3 °C.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 3
{{sp[info] Objective 11.1a}} · *short answer* Acetone ($\ce{(CH3)2CO}$) cannot hydrogen-bond with itself, yet it dissolves readily in water. Explain both facts.
:::
::: tab Answer
**Why it cannot hydrogen-bond with itself:** hydrogen bonding needs both a donor (H bonded directly to N, O, or F) and an acceptor (a lone pair on N, O, or F). Acetone has an excellent acceptor — the carbonyl oxygen's lone pairs — but no donor, because all six of its hydrogens sit on carbon. With only acceptors and no donors, acetone molecules cannot hydrogen-bond to one another; they are held together by dipole-dipole and dispersion forces.

**Why it dissolves in water:** water supplies the missing donor. A water O–H hydrogen bonds to acetone's carbonyl oxygen, so acetone hydrogen-bonds *with water* even though it cannot with itself. This donor/acceptor asymmetry is the general rule for ethers, ketones, aldehydes, and esters — all water-soluble, none self-hydrogen-bonding.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 4
{{sp[info] Objective 11.1b}} · *workout* Rank $\ce{Ne}$, $\ce{Ar}$, and $\ce{Kr}$ in order of increasing boiling point, and justify the order.
:::
::: tab Answer
All three are nonpolar monatomic noble gases, so only dispersion forces apply. Dispersion force strength increases with polarizability, which increases with the number of electrons: Ne (10 electrons) < Ar (18 electrons) < Kr (36 electrons).

$$\ce{Ne} < \ce{Ar} < \ce{Kr}$$

(Actual boiling points: Ne −246.1 °C, Ar −185.8 °C, Kr −153.2 °C — confirming the predicted order.)
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 5
{{sp[info] Objective 11.1b}} · *applied* Decane ($\ce{C10H22}$, nonpolar) boils at 174 °C, while hydrogen chloride ($\ce{HCl}$, polar) boils at −85 °C. Explain why the nonpolar substance boils at a much higher temperature.
:::
::: tab Answer
Boiling point depends on total intermolecular force strength, not on polarity alone. Decane is nonpolar and has only dispersion forces, but its large size and high electron count make those dispersion forces substantial — collectively stronger than HCl's smaller dipole-dipole + dispersion forces. This is the size/polarizability exception to the general polar-beats-nonpolar ranking.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 6
{{sp[info] Objective 11.1b}} · *multiple-choice* Which list places the four attraction types in order of **decreasing** typical strength?

(A) ion-dipole > hydrogen bonding > dipole-dipole > dispersion
(B) hydrogen bonding > ion-dipole > dispersion > dipole-dipole
\(C) dipole-dipole > hydrogen bonding > ion-dipole > dispersion
(D) dispersion > dipole-dipole > hydrogen bonding > ion-dipole
:::
::: tab Answer
**(A)** Typical magnitudes: ion-dipole 40–600 kJ/mol, hydrogen bonding 10–40 kJ/mol, dipole-dipole 2–5 kJ/mol, dispersion 0.05–40 kJ/mol.

The one caveat worth remembering is that dispersion has the widest range of the four. For a small molecule it is negligible; for a large, highly polarizable one it can exceed hydrogen bonding outright — which is why $\ce{I2}$ is a solid while $\ce{H2O}$, a hydrogen-bonded substance, is only a liquid. The ranking above describes *typical* cases, not a law that holds molecule by molecule.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 7
{{sp[info] Objective 11.2a}} · *short answer* Glycerin ($\ce{C3H8O3}$, with three O–H groups per molecule) is far more viscous than water at room temperature. Explain why.
:::
::: tab Answer
Each glycerin molecule can form multiple hydrogen bonds (three O–H groups vs. water's two), creating a more extensive hydrogen-bonding network per molecule. This stronger intermolecular attraction makes it much harder for glycerin molecules to slide past one another, producing much higher viscosity than water.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 8
{{sp[info] Objective 11.2a}} · *conceptual* In a thin glass tube, water rises above the surrounding liquid level, while mercury is depressed below it. What does this tell you about the relative strength of cohesion and adhesion for each liquid?
:::
::: tab Answer
For water: adhesion (water–glass attraction) exceeds cohesion (water–water attraction), so the liquid climbs the tube walls. For mercury: cohesion (strong metallic-like attraction between mercury atoms) exceeds adhesion (mercury–glass attraction), so the liquid pulls away from the walls and is depressed at the center.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 9
{{sp[info] Objective 11.2a}} · *applied* Mercury forms a *convex* (dome-shaped) meniscus in a glass tube, while water forms a *concave* one. Explain the difference in terms of cohesion and adhesion, and state which liquid will rise in a capillary tube.
:::
::: tab Answer
The shape of a meniscus is decided by which is stronger: **cohesion** (liquid-to-liquid) or **adhesion** (liquid-to-glass).

**Water:** adhesion to the polar Si–OH groups on the glass surface exceeds cohesion between water molecules, so water climbs the walls and its surface curves *upward* at the edges — a **concave** meniscus. Water will rise in a capillary tube.

**Mercury:** metallic bonding between mercury atoms is far stronger than any attraction between mercury and glass, so cohesion wins. Mercury pulls away from the walls and beads inward — a **convex** meniscus. Mercury is actually *depressed* in a capillary tube rather than rising in it.

**Practical consequence:** read a water meniscus at the bottom of its curve, but read a mercury one at the top — the reading rule from Chapter 1 follows directly from which force wins here.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 10
{{sp[info] Objective 11.2b}} · *short answer* Explain, at the molecular level, why ice is less dense than liquid water.
:::
::: tab Answer
In ice, each water molecule is locked into a rigid, hydrogen-bonded lattice that holds neighboring molecules at a fixed, relatively open (spacious) arrangement to maximize the number of hydrogen bonds. In liquid water, molecules are not locked in place and can pack somewhat more closely together on average. The more open solid structure gives ice a lower density than the liquid.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 11
{{sp[info] Objective 11.2b}} · *applied* Coastal cities generally have smaller day-to-night and summer-to-winter temperature swings than inland cities at the same latitude. Explain this in terms of one of water's anomalous properties.
:::
::: tab Answer
Water has an unusually high specific heat (4.184 J/g·°C) due to its extensive hydrogen bonding. Large bodies of water near coastal cities absorb or release large amounts of heat with only small temperature changes, moderating the surrounding air temperature and reducing extreme swings compared to inland areas without a large nearby water reservoir.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 12
{{sp[info] Objective 11.2b}} · *short answer* Coastal cities have far milder temperature swings between day and night, and between summer and winter, than inland cities at the same latitude. Explain how one of water's hydrogen-bonding-derived anomalies accounts for this.
:::
::: tab Answer
The relevant anomaly is water's **unusually high specific heat** (4.184 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ — among the highest of any common liquid).

Heat added to water goes partly into breaking and rearranging hydrogen bonds rather than entirely into increasing molecular kinetic energy. Since temperature measures kinetic energy, a large amount of heat produces only a small temperature rise, and the reverse holds on cooling.

A large body of water therefore acts as a thermal buffer: it absorbs solar energy through the day and summer with little warming, then releases it slowly through the night and winter with little cooling. Land, with a specific heat roughly one-fifth of water's, heats and cools quickly by comparison, so inland air temperature tracks the sun much more closely.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 13
{{sp[info] Objective 11.3a}} · *multiple-choice* Quartz ($\ce{SiO2}$) is best classified as which type of solid?

(A) Molecular
(B) Covalent network
\(C) Ionic
(D) Metallic
:::
::: tab Answer
**(B)** Every silicon and oxygen atom in quartz is linked by covalent bonds into one continuous three-dimensional network — there are no discrete molecules and no free-moving ions or delocalized metallic electrons. This gives quartz its characteristic hardness and very high melting point.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 14
{{sp[info] Objective 11.3a}} · *short answer* Diamond and graphite are both covalent-network forms of pure carbon, yet graphite conducts electricity and diamond does not. Explain the difference.
:::
::: tab Answer
In diamond, every carbon atom is $sp^3$-hybridized and forms four localized single bonds — all electrons are tied up in fixed bonds with nowhere to move, so diamond does not conduct. In graphite, each carbon is $sp^2$-hybridized, forming three bonds within a flat sheet plus a leftover, delocalized $p$ electron shared across the whole sheet. Those delocalized electrons are free to move, which is why graphite conducts electricity (well within its layers) despite being, like diamond, a covalent-network solid.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 15
{{sp[info] Objective 11.3a}} · *applied* Both diamond and graphite are pure carbon and both are covalent-network solids, yet diamond is the hardest natural substance and an electrical insulator while graphite is soft enough to write with and conducts electricity. Account for both differences.
:::
::: tab Answer
Same element, different **network geometry** — a demonstration that structure, not composition, sets a solid's properties.

**Diamond:** every carbon is $sp^3$-hybridized and covalently bonded to four others in a rigid three-dimensional tetrahedral network. Deforming the crystal in any direction requires breaking covalent bonds, hence extreme hardness. All four valence electrons are localized in $\sigma$ bonds, so none are free to move — an insulator.

**Graphite:** every carbon is $sp^2$-hybridized and bonded to three others in flat hexagonal sheets. Within a sheet the bonding is very strong, but the sheets are held to one another only by **dispersion forces**, so they slide past each other easily — soft, and useful as a lubricant and as pencil "lead." The leftover fourth electron per atom occupies a delocalized $\pi$ system spread across each sheet, and those mobile electrons conduct electricity *along* the sheets.

Note that graphite's softness comes from an *intermolecular* force between sheets, not from weak covalent bonding — the covalent bonds inside a graphite sheet are actually shorter and stronger than diamond's.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 16
{{sp[info] Objective 11.3b}} · *workout* How many atoms belong to one face-centered cubic (FCC) unit cell? Show the sharing-fraction arithmetic.
:::
::: tab Answer
FCC has 8 corner atoms and 6 face atoms.

$$\text{Corners: } 8 \times \frac{1}{8} = 1\ \text{atom}$$
$$\text{Faces: } 6 \times \frac{1}{2} = 3\ \text{atoms}$$
$$\text{Total} = 1 + 3 = 4\ \text{atoms per FCC unit cell}$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 17
{{sp[info] Objective 11.3b}} · *inverse* A cubic unit cell has a coordination number of 8. Which cubic cell type is this, and how many atoms does it contain?
:::
::: tab Answer
Coordination number 8 identifies a **body-centered cubic (BCC)** cell (atoms touch along the cube's body diagonal). A BCC cell contains 2 atoms per cell (1 from the 8 shared corners, plus 1 full atom at the body center).
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 18
{{sp[info] Objective 11.3b}} · *workout* Silver crystallizes in a face-centered cubic lattice with an edge length of 409 pm. Determine the number of atoms per unit cell, then calculate the density of silver. (Molar mass 107.87 g/mol.)
:::
::: tab Answer
**Step 1 — atoms per cell.** FCC has atoms at 8 corners (each shared among 8 cells) and 6 face centers (each shared between 2 cells):
$$8\left(\tfrac{1}{8}\right) + 6\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = 1 + 3 = 4\ \text{atoms}$$

**Step 2 — mass in one cell.**
$$m = \frac{4\ \text{atoms} \times 107.87\ \text{g/mol}}{6.022\times10^{23}\ \text{atoms/mol}} = 7.165\times10^{-22}\ \text{g}$$

**Step 3 — volume of the cell.** Convert the edge to centimeters: $409\ \text{pm} = 4.09\times10^{-8}$ cm.
$$V = (4.09\times10^{-8})^3 = 6.842\times10^{-23}\ \text{cm}^3$$

**Step 4 — density.**
$$d = \frac{7.165\times10^{-22}\ \text{g}}{6.842\times10^{-23}\ \text{cm}^3} = 10.5\ \text{g/cm}^3$$

The accepted density of silver is 10.49 g/cm³ — a good check that the atom count was right. Had you used 1 atom per cell (simple cubic) the answer would have come out four times too small, so the density calculation doubles as a test of the packing assumption.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 19
{{sp[info] Objective 11.4a}} · *workout* The molar heat of vaporization of ethanol ($\ce{C2H5OH}$, molar mass 46.07 g/mol) is 38.6 kJ/mol. How much heat is required to vaporize 25.0 g of ethanol at its boiling point?
:::
::: tab Answer
First convert mass to moles:

$$25.0\ \text{g}\ \ce{C2H5OH} \times \frac{1\ \text{mol}}{46.07\ \text{g}} = 0.543\ \text{mol}$$

Then multiply by the molar heat of vaporization:

$$0.543\ \text{mol} \times 38.6\ \text{kJ/mol} = 20.9\ \text{kJ}$$

**20.9 kJ** of heat must be absorbed to vaporize this sample.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 20
{{sp[info] Objective 11.4a}} · *workout* How much heat is released when 45.0 g of steam at 100 °C condenses and then cools to 25 °C? ($\Delta H_\text{vap} = 40.66$ kJ/mol, $s_\text{water} = 4.184$ J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹.)
:::
::: tab Answer
Two steps, both releasing heat, so both are negative from the water's point of view.

$$n = \frac{45.0\ \text{g}}{18.02\ \text{g/mol}} = 2.497\ \text{mol}$$

**Step 1 — condense at 100 °C** (the reverse of vaporization, so the sign flips):
$$q_1 = -(2.497)(40.66) = -101.5\ \text{kJ}$$

**Step 2 — cool the liquid from 100 to 25 °C:**
$$q_2 = (45.0)(4.184)(25.0 - 100.0) = -14{,}121\ \text{J} = -14.1\ \text{kJ}$$

$$q_\text{total} = -101.5 + (-14.1) = -116\ \text{kJ}$$

**Why steam burns are so much worse than hot-water burns:** condensation alone dumps 101.5 kJ — over seven times the energy released by cooling the same mass through 75 degrees. Skin contacted by 100 °C steam receives all of that before the liquid even begins to cool.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 21
{{sp[info] Objective 11.4a}} · *multiple-choice* A sealed flask holds liquid diethyl ether in equilibrium with its vapor at 20 °C. You pour out half the liquid, reseal the flask, and return it to 20 °C. What happens to the equilibrium vapor pressure?

(A) It falls to half its original value
(B) It falls, but by less than half
\(C) It is unchanged
(D) It rises, because there is more space for vapor
:::
::: tab Answer
**\(C)** Equilibrium vapor pressure depends only on the **substance's identity and the temperature** — never on how much liquid is present or how large the container is.

At equilibrium, the rate of evaporation depends on the surface area *per unit of surface*, and the rate of condensation depends on the vapor's pressure. Halving the liquid does not change the temperature, so molecules still escape with the same distribution of energies, and equilibrium re-establishes at the same pressure. The only thing that changes is how long the liquid will last before it is entirely gone.

**(A)** and **(B)** treat vapor pressure as an extensive property, which it is not. **(D)** confuses vapor pressure with the behavior of a fixed amount of gas being expanded.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 22
{{sp[info] Objective 11.4b}} · *workout* Water's vapor pressure is 23.8 mmHg at 25 °C, and its molar heat of vaporization is 40.66 kJ/mol. Use the Clausius–Clapeyron equation to estimate the temperature at which water's vapor pressure reaches 760 mmHg (i.e., estimate its normal boiling point).
:::
::: tab Answer
Using $\ln\left(\dfrac{P_2}{P_1}\right) = -\dfrac{\Delta H_\text{vap}}{R}\left(\dfrac{1}{T_2} - \dfrac{1}{T_1}\right)$ with $T_1 = 298.15\ \text{K}$, $P_1 = 23.8\ \text{mmHg}$, $P_2 = 760\ \text{mmHg}$:

$$\ln\left(\frac{760}{23.8}\right) = 3.464 = -\frac{40{,}660}{8.314}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{298.15}\right)$$

Solving for $T_2$ gives $T_2 \approx 378\ \text{K} = 105\ \text{°C}$.

This is close to, but not exactly, water's true normal boiling point of 100 °C — the Clausius–Clapeyron equation assumes $\Delta H_\text{vap}$ is constant with temperature, which is only approximately true, so a few degrees of deviation from a single-$\Delta H_\text{vap}$ calculation is expected and normal.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 23
{{sp[info] Objective 11.4b}} · *workout* Water has $\Delta H_\text{vap} = 40.66$ kJ/mol and a normal boiling point of 100 °C (where its vapor pressure is 760 mmHg). Calculate water's vapor pressure at 25 °C.
:::
::: tab Answer
Use the two-point Clausius–Clapeyron equation with the known point as state 1:

$$\ln\frac{P_1}{P_2} = \frac{\Delta H_\text{vap}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right)$$

$P_1 = 760$ mmHg, $T_1 = 373.15$ K, $T_2 = 298.15$ K, $R = 8.314$ J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

$$\frac{1}{298.15} - \frac{1}{373.15} = 0.0033540 - 0.0026799 = 6.741\times10^{-4}\ \text{K}^{-1}$$
$$\ln\frac{760}{P_2} = \frac{40{,}660}{8.314}\left(6.741\times10^{-4}\right) = (4890.5)(6.741\times10^{-4}) = 3.297$$
$$\frac{760}{P_2} = e^{3.297} = 27.03 \quad\Rightarrow\quad P_2 = \frac{760}{27.03} = 28.1\ \text{mmHg}$$

The measured value at 25 °C is 23.8 mmHg, so the estimate is about 18% high — the usual consequence of assuming $\Delta H_\text{vap}$ stays constant across a 75-degree span.

**Unit reminder:** $\Delta H_\text{vap}$ must be in **joules** per mole to match $R = 8.314$. Leaving it in kJ gives an exponent a thousand times too small.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 24
{{sp[info] Objective 11.4b}} · *short answer* A plot of $\ln P$ against $1/T$ for a pure liquid gives a straight line. What does the slope of that line represent, and what does a *steeper* (more negative) slope tell you about the liquid?
:::
::: tab Answer
Rearranged into slope-intercept form, the Clausius–Clapeyron equation reads

$$\ln P = -\frac{\Delta H_\text{vap}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T}\right) + C$$

so plotting $\ln P$ (y) against $1/T$ (x) gives a straight line of slope $-\Delta H_\text{vap}/R$. Multiplying the measured slope by $-R$ therefore yields the molar heat of vaporization — which is how $\Delta H_\text{vap}$ is determined experimentally, using many data points rather than the two-point shortcut.

**A steeper (more negative) slope means a larger $\Delta H_\text{vap}$**, and therefore **stronger intermolecular forces**. Practically, such a liquid's vapor pressure is more sensitive to temperature and it is less volatile at any given temperature. Water's plot is steeper than diethyl ether's for exactly this reason.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 25
{{sp[info] Objective 11.4c}} · *short answer* Using the phase diagram of water, describe what happens if you start at a pressure of 0.5 kPa (well below atmospheric) and slowly raise the temperature from −20 °C, keeping pressure fixed at 0.5 kPa.
:::
::: tab Answer
At 0.5 kPa (about 0.005 atm), this pressure is close to but just below the triple-point pressure (0.00604 atm ≈ 0.612 kPa). Starting in the solid region and raising temperature at this low, roughly triple-point-adjacent pressure, water sublimes directly from solid to vapor without passing through a liquid phase — because 0.5 kPa is below the pressure needed to stabilize liquid water at any temperature along this path.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 26
{{sp[info] Objective 11.4c}} · *applied* Freeze-drying preserves food by removing water without ever letting it melt. Using a phase diagram, explain the two conditions the process requires and why the food is not damaged.
:::
::: tab Answer
Freeze-drying is **sublimation performed deliberately**, which on a phase diagram means keeping the sample below the triple point at all times.

**Condition 1 — freeze the food first**, putting it in the solid region well left of 0 °C.

**Condition 2 — pump the pressure below water's triple-point pressure** (0.00604 atm ≈ 4.6 mmHg). Below that pressure, no liquid region exists at any temperature: a horizontal path across the diagram crosses only the solid–vapor boundary. Warming the sample gently under vacuum therefore drives ice directly to vapor, which is pumped away.

**Why the food survives:** liquid water is what does the damage. It dissolves and carries away flavor compounds, supports the chemical reactions and microbial growth that cause spoilage, and its surface tension collapses cell walls as it evaporates. Sublimation skips the liquid phase entirely, so the solid structure is left behind intact and porous — which is also why freeze-dried food rehydrates so quickly.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 27
{{sp[info] Objective 11.4c}} · *short answer* Ice skating is often explained by saying the skate's pressure melts the ice beneath the blade. Using water's phase diagram, evaluate whether that explanation can be correct.
:::
::: tab Answer
The explanation is **directionally right about the diagram but quantitatively wrong**, and it is worth working out why.

**What the diagram does support:** water's solid–liquid boundary has a *negative* slope, because ice is less dense than liquid water. Increasing pressure therefore favors the denser liquid and *lowers* the melting point. Water is one of the very few substances for which pressure-induced melting is even possible in principle — for a normal substance with a positive-sloped boundary, pressure would freeze the liquid, not melt the solid.

**Why it still fails:** the boundary is very nearly vertical. Depressing water's melting point by even 1 °C requires roughly 130 atm. A skater's blade, though narrow, produces on the order of tens of atmospheres — enough for a few hundredths of a degree, nowhere near enough to melt ice at a typical rink temperature of −5 °C.

**The accepted explanation** combines frictional heating from the moving blade with a pre-existing quasi-liquid surface layer that exists on ice even without applied pressure. The pressure-melting story survives in textbooks because the phase diagram makes it *plausible*; checking the magnitude is what rules it out.
:::
::::
